Written in 1976 as an early, rejected treatment of the 2-3-74 material Dick later reworked into VALIS; the two novels share substantial autobiographical and theological content but differ in narrative frame and ending.

reading.synopsis: In an alternate United States under the increasingly authoritarian rule of President Ferris F. Fremont, science fiction writer Nicholas Brady begins receiving communications from a satellite intelligence he comes to believe is VALIS, transmitting information -- including the correct diagnosis of a life-threatening birth defect in his infant son -- that he has no ordinary way of knowing. Nicholas shares his experience with his friend, a struggling science fiction writer named Philip (a thinly fictionalized version of Dick himself), who becomes his chronicler and, increasingly, a fellow believer as Fremont's government grows more openly repressive, hunting dissidents through a surveillance and disinformation apparatus that frames ordinary political opposition as un-American subversion. The novel builds to Nicholas's arrest and death as a suspected subversive after VALIS guides him toward acts of resistance against Fremont's regime, with Philip left to record and interpret what happened, uncertain whether Nicholas was a genuine instrument of divine or extraterrestrial intervention or a delusional casualty of a paranoid, authoritarian political moment.

reading.significance: Radio Free Albemuth is Dick's first attempt to fictionalize his 1974 religious/visionary experience, written in 1976 and rejected by his publisher, who asked for a substantially different book -- the rejection that led Dick to write VALIS instead, reworking much of the same autobiographical and theological material into a different narrative frame. Published posthumously in 1985, the novel is frequently studied alongside VALIS as a comparative case study in how Dick's treatment of the same core experience shifted between drafts: Radio Free Albemuth splits the autobiographical material between two characters (Nicholas and Philip) rather than fusing them into VALIS's single unstable narrator, and frames the theological material more explicitly through an authoritarian political allegory targeting the Nixon-era surveillance state.
reading.closing_note: Philip's final uncertainty about whether Nicholas was a genuine instrument of transcendent contact or a delusional casualty of political paranoia leaves the novel's central theological question as open as Dick's own lifelong ambivalence about the nature of his 1974 experience.
